tagline: From Mediterranean shores to Saharan dunes
overview:
Algeria is the largest country in Africa and the tenth largest in the world, covering about 2.4 million square kilometers, more than three times the size of Texas. Yet most of that land is the Sahara, and the great majority of its roughly 45 million people live in a narrow green strip along the Mediterranean coast. The capital, Algiers, climbs a hillside in tiers of white buildings, earning it the nickname Algiers the White.

Arabic is the official language, alongside Tamazight, the language of the Berber (Amazigh) peoples who lived here long before Arabic arrived. French, left behind from colonial times, is still widely used in business and schools. Algeria is a republic led by a president, and its economy depends heavily on oil and natural gas pumped from beneath the desert. Cities are modern and busy, while oasis towns in the south keep centuries-old rhythms shaped by date harvests and the heat.
landAndNature: Two mountain chains, the Tell Atlas and the Saharan Atlas, run parallel to the coast with a belt of high plateaus between them. South of the mountains the Sahara takes over for more than 80 percent of the country. It is not all sand: there are seas of dunes called ergs, gravel plains, and the rocky Hoggar Mountains, where Mount Tahat rises to about 2,900 meters. The Tassili n'Ajjer plateau is a maze of sandstone pillars and arches. Algeria's national animal is the fennec fox, whose enormous ears release heat and pick up the faint sounds of prey under the sand. Dorcas gazelles, Barbary macaques in the northern cedar forests, and a tiny population of Saharan cheetahs also survive here.
peopleAndCulture: Most Algerians have both Arab and Berber ancestry, and Berber groups such as the Kabyle, Chaoui, and Tuareg keep their own languages and traditions. Nearly everyone is Muslim, and the weekend falls on Friday and Saturday. Couscous, steamed grains topped with vegetables and meat, is the national dish, joined by chorba soup, spicy merguez sausages, and honey-soaked makroud pastries. Sweet mint tea is offered to every guest. Raï, a lively pop music born in the port city of Oran, is famous across the Arab world and beyond. Soccer is a passion: the national team, the Desert Foxes, won the Africa Cup of Nations in 1990 and 2019. The writer Albert Camus, who won the Nobel Prize, was born in Algeria.
history: Berber kingdoms such as Numidia flourished here more than 2,000 years ago, trading and sometimes fighting with Carthage and Rome, whose ruins still stand at Timgad and Djemila. Arab armies brought Islam in the 7th century, and the Ottoman Empire later controlled the coast. France invaded in 1830 and ruled Algeria as part of France for 132 years, settling over a million Europeans on the best farmland. A brutal war of independence from 1954 to 1962 cost hundreds of thousands of lives before Algeria became free on July 5, 1962. One party governed for decades, and a civil war in the 1990s killed tens of thousands. Huge peaceful protests in 2019 led the long-serving president to resign.
funFacts: The rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer includes thousands of paintings, some up to 12,000 years old, showing giraffes and cattle in what is now desert.
Algeria is bigger than all of Western Europe's largest countries, France, Spain, Germany, and Italy, put together.
The Sahara's Grand Erg Oriental, a sea of dunes, is larger than the entire country of Ireland.
Ghardaïa, an oasis city in the M'zab valley, has kept the same pyramid-like layout for about a thousand years.
The Casbah of Algiers, a steep tangle of alleys and stairways from Ottoman times, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
